transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Giles Snyder.
President Trump is back from his trip to Asia and says he will hold a press conference at the White House later today
to discuss the trip in which he participated in the first ever trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian leader Vladimir Putin.
And here's Franco Ordonez.
That is being made already of how Trump interacted with the two leaders.
And we need to remember that Xi and Putin are economic adversaries. They're accused human rights abusers.
And of course, other U.S. presidents have met and been cordial with world leaders.
But it is different with Trump, basically because he doesn't act that way with longtime allies.
I mean, it's really just such a stark contrast.
European leaders have expressed concern about Trump's meeting in China.
They met in Berlin Thursday as they pushed to be included in the U.S. back talks to end the war in Ukraine,
seeking to reassure Europe.
U.S. envoy Jared Kushner attended the Berlin meeting and said Trump is open to NATO-like security guarantees for a postwar Ukraine,
and that he believes Russia is comfortable with that.
The Senate has rejected a measure aimed at reining in President Trump's Iran war.
And here's Barbara Sproun reports.
The Senate voted against a House-adopted measure that would direct President Trump to remove U.S. armed forces from hostilities with Iran.
It was a largely party-line vote.
Three Republicans, Senators Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, and Rand Paul of Kentucky,
voted with Democrats in favor of the resolution.
All Democrats supported it except Pennsylvania Senator John Federman.
Had it passed, it would have largely been symbolic.
Administrations from both parties have long sidestepped Congress in terms of war powers.
Barbara Sproun, NPR News, The Capitol.
The Senate has passed a bipartisan bill aimed at speeding up the permitting process for the construction of new power plants,
transmission lines, and other energy infrastructure in a bid to meet demand and lower electricity prices.
That bill now goes to the House, which passed a limited version last year.
U.S. Army delaying the detonation of several tons of bomb-making chemicals in southeast Iowa following public safety concerns.
The decision came Thursday evening after two environmental groups filed a lawsuit seeking emergency court action to stop the plan out of concern about exposure to lead dust.
Iowa Public Radio's Eliza Billingham has more.
The announcement on social media said Monday was the latest moment possible before a temperature drop.
Army spokesperson Justine Berati warns that cold weather could make the situation even more dangerous.
The primary concern that we have right now is that lead azides can become more volatile when it is exposed to lower temperatures.
The Army says it will run new models based on Monday's forecast and provide updated maps of areas of greatest impact.
You're listening to NPR News. The president of FIFA will face two challengers in the upcoming election to head the world soccer body.
But NPR's Rafael Naum reports that Gianni Infantino appears well placed to win another term.
The president of the French Football Federation, Philippe Diallo, and Japanese soccer official Kozo Tashima are officially running in the FIFA elections scheduled for mid-March.
By the tally by the Associated Press, shows Infantino is only a vote short of the threshold needed to be re-elected, based on endorsements from soccer federations around the world.
It's a remarkable comeback after Infantino sparked major controversy after working on a secret plan to sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors.
Infantino quickly abandoned the proposal and has been traveling around the world to make amends. Rafael Naum, NPR News.
The White House has a new national cybersecurity director. The administration has tapped the Pentagon's chief information officer, Kirsten Davies, to at least temporarily replace Sean Cairncross after President Trump faced criticism over a cascade of tech outages that affected air travel, banking, and classified communications.
Condolences have been pouring in after the Cincinnati Zoo's announcement that Fiona the Hippo has died.
The zoo says Fiona died Thursday after swallowing a knit hat that had been accidentally thrown into her enclosure more than a week ago.
The zoo says Fiona died after multiple attempts to help her. She was nine years old, captivated people worldwide after her premature birth in 2017.

topics.text: Trump returns from Asia trip, plans White House press conference on meetings with Xi and Putin
European leaders meet in Berlin to press for inclusion in US talks on ending Ukraine war
Senate rejects House-passed measure directing Trump to remove forces from Iran hostilities
Senate passes bipartisan bill to speed permitting for power plants and transmission lines
Army delays detonation of bomb-making chemicals in southeast Iowa over lead dust concerns
FIFA presidential election: Infantino appears well placed to win re-election against two challengers
White House names Pentagon CIO Kirsten Davies as acting national cybersecurity director
Cincinnati Zoo announces death of Fiona the Hippo after she swallowed a knit hat
